## The one-paragraph version

There were 38 grandfathered bespoke state reads. They answer about **8 questions**. That
gap — not the size of the tool catalog — is what "which tool do I call?" actually is, and
it is what the cell registry exists to close. Of the 38: **7 own a derivation and become
cells**, **8 re-derive a value someone else owns and must delegate**, and **23 correctly
stay bespoke**. The verdicts are not in this page; they are in
`scripts/check-no-bespoke-state-read.mjs` as a `VERDICTS` map keyed to the same `BASELINE`
the gate enforces, so "every grandfathered tool has a verdict" is a CI-checked property
rather than a claim. This page is the argument behind them.

## Current authority: measurement plus explicit assessment

The inventory still answers which doors collapse into shared cells, but the consumer contract has changed. A readable poll cell exposes two separate properties from one resolver payload:

- **Measurement** is the existing headline/raw value. It keeps its stable type for thresholds, predicates, auditing, dependency digests, and debugging.
- **Assessment** is the resolver-owned, closed enum at `assessment.path`. Each code declares its meaning, safe action, and same-payload evidence. It is the first decision surface; callers do not reconstruct a conclusion by negating a warning or by guessing from the measurement.

The registry validates and transports that declaration; it does not derive domain meaning. A resolved `state:read { cell }` therefore returns the raw measurement and its explicit assessment together. If assessment evidence is missing, a code is unknown, or the resolver is not measurable, the read is explicitly `unknown`/`unavailable` with a reread lever. Unknown is not false, zero, or healthy.

Use the shared doors at the moment of action:

```text
state:read { cell: "git.pipelinePosition", as: "<path when required>" }
state:subscribe { cell: "git.pipelinePosition" }  // semantic change by default
state:subscribe { cell: "git.pipelinePosition", target: "measurement", on: { op: "changed" } }
```

`state:subscribe` without `on` means “wake when the meaning moves” for an assessed cell. A valued predicate must name `target: "assessment"` or `target: "measurement"`; the tool refuses an ambiguous operand rather than comparing it against a guessed path. `target: "material"` remains an explicit opt-in where the cell declares a materiality lens. Event-signalled cells have no resolver to poll and redirect to their declared `events:await` key.

Delivery-time payloads use the same contract. A `state-plane` stamp names a cell and emits a `state:read` reread handle for the exact subject; it does not copy the value, invent an assessment, or provide a second subscription mechanism. Re-read immediately before acting or quoting the value, preserving `as` for caller-relative cells.

### Supersession boundary (P-007 / D-006)

The assessment contract supersedes only the axis-one falsifier clauses and their registration refinement in `unified-agent-state-plane-2026-07-27`, plus the delivery-time push-falsifier requirement in `state-plane-interest-and-hardening-2026-08-21`. Those historical decisions remain readable as history. All other axes remain effective: in-band unknowns and hoists, caller relativity, provenance, one derivation with many lenses, access/federation, materiality, ordered stages, and delivery-time reread discipline. The positive assessment/evidence contract is now authoritative on pull, push, and subscription paths.

## Why the verdicts are not written down here

The obvious deliverable for "inventory the state reads and give each a verdict" is a
table in a document. That is the wrong artifact, for the reason this whole plan exists:
a table in a doc is a **transcription** of `BASELINE`, and it starts drifting from
`BASELINE` the first time `BASELINE` changes. An inventory that silently disagrees with
the set it describes is worse than no inventory, because it reads authoritative.

So the verdict lives beside the thing it describes:

```js
export const VERDICTS = new Map([
  ['coord:presence', { verdict: 'cell', cluster: 'presence', calls: 648, reason: '…' }],
  …
]);
```

and `verdictGaps()` fails the gate if a grandfathered tool has no verdict, if a verdict
names a tool that is not grandfathered, if a verdict has an unknown kind, or if its
reason is short enough to be a rubber stamp. Retiring a tool has to update both maps or
CI goes red.

One carve-out matters. A verdict **may** outlive its baseline entry, but only if it
records *how* the tool left, in an `adopted` note held to the same minimum length as an
exemption reason. Without that, the inventory would erode exactly as the work succeeded —
every retirement deleting the record of what was decided and why. With it, `BASELINE`
shrinks (the ratchet) while `VERDICTS` accumulates the history.

## The three verdicts

They are deliberately non-overlapping, and they are D-038 axis 5 ("one derivation, many
lenses") applied per tool.

| verdict | meaning | what happens |
|---|---|---|
| `cell` | the tool **owns** a live-state derivation that other surfaces re-derive | register the cell(s) here; the tool declares `@cell-lens` over its own resolver |
| `delegates` | the tool **re-derives** a value another tool owns | it must consume the cell instead of computing a second answer |
| `bespoke` | stays as it is | with a stated reason |

`cell` tools are the **resolvers**. `delegates` tools are the **duplication sites**, and
therefore the refactor and retirement candidates. If you are looking for where the work
is, it is the `delegates` column.

## The discipline that keeps the registry from becoming surface #29

This is the part most likely to be got wrong by a well-meaning successor, so it is
stated as a rule rather than left to taste.

> **A read can be genuinely live state and still correctly stay bespoke.**

If exactly one tool answers a question and nothing re-derives it, promoting it to a cell
**adds a registry entry without removing a door**. That is precisely the D-010 failure
the plan opens with: `predicate_watches` shipped, correct in principle, 0 rows across all
tenants — a registry nobody registers into is not neutral, it is one more place to look.
The registry earns its keep by collapsing *duplicated* doors, not by cataloguing every
read.

The same logic kills the tempting move of promoting everything with a `status` in its
name: **a read with 0 calls in 30 days is never promoted**. Registering a value nobody
asks for is the `predicate_watches` failure at cell scale. Eight of the 38 baseline
entries have zero calls; none became a cell.

This is why the rollup is `7 cell · 8 delegates · 23 bespoke` and not `38 cells`, and
why the unit test asserts `bespoke > cell` — a registry that swallowed everything would
be the failure mode, not the goal.

## The evidence the verdicts were assigned from

Two dimensions, both measured rather than judged.

**Call volume** (`tool_invocations`, 30d, 2026-07-27 — note the table's retention is
about 30 days, so `calls_all == calls_30d` for every row):

| tool | calls | distinct callers |
|---|---|---|
| `coord:presence` | 648 | 635 |
| `dev:pipeline_position` | 310 | 288 |
| `fleet:status` | 263 | 256 |
| `pot:status` | 202 | 202 |
| `accounts:status` | 179 | 179 |
| `fleet:capacity` | 144 | 144 |
| `dev:service_health` | 134 | 126 |
| `events:status` | 121 | 121 |
| …29 more, tailing to 0 | | |

**The shape that matters is the ratio.** `calls ≈ distinct callers` on nearly every hot
entry — 202/202, 179/179, 144/144, 121/121. These are **once-per-session orientation
reads**: every agent asks exactly once, on waking, and never again. That is the cell
shape, and it is the strongest single piece of evidence that the clustering below is real
rather than aesthetic. A tool with 500 calls from 3 callers would be a hot *loop*, which
is a different problem with a different fix (`state:subscribe`, not `state:read`).

**Resolver eligibility**, which constrains *how* a cell can be registered rather than
whether it should be:

- `effect` is **inferred**, not declared — write-ish capability suffixes
  (`:write`/`:admin`/`:delete`/`:manage`/`:execute`) or the `WRITE_CAPABILITIES` set mean
  `write`; everything else means `read` (`libs/generic/tooldef/src/define-tool.ts`). None
  of the 38 declares `effect` inline and all 38 infer `read`, so **effect is not the
  constraint** — every one of them is eligible as a resolver.
- The real constraint is caller-relativity. A cell declaring `callerRelativity: 'global'`
  is dispatched with `{}`, so its resolver **must answer bare**. Exactly 6 of the 38
  require an argument — `accounts:link-status`, `egress:health`, `fleet:status`,
  `harness:health`, `plan_items:status`, `watchdog:status` — and are therefore
  `parameter`-relative, not global. The other 32 answer bare.

> ⚠ Two traps worth inheriting. First, a tool's argument schema field is **`args:`**, not
> `input:` — an extractor keyed on `input:` reports "takes no arguments" for *every* tool
> and looks entirely plausible. Second, this exact mistake already shipped once: three
> global cells resolved to `insufficient-data` because `dev:pipeline_position` rejected a
> no-arg call (D-067 defect 2, fixed in P-007). Before promising any global cell, check
> its resolver answers `{}` — or it registers dead, and a registration that reads as an
> error is worse than no registration.

## The finding: 38 tools, ~8 questions

| # | the question agents are actually asking | doors | calls/30d |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | can I get inference capacity right now? | `fleet:capacity` · `accounts:status` · `gateway:status` · `dev:rate_governor_status` · `egress:health` · `accounts:link-status` · `setup:status` | 431 |
| B | who is alive, and on what? | `coord:presence` · `fleet:status` · `scheduler:running` · `plan_items:status` (+ the annex below) | 963 |
| C | is my code live? | `dev:pipeline_position` · `dev:build_status` · `deploy:status` | 390 |
| D | is the box / service healthy? | `dev:service_health` · `dev:pg_health` · `dev:processes` · `dev:dogfood_substrate_status` · `harness:health` · `storage:usage` · `dev:listening_ports` | 170 |
| E | is the background machinery running? | `events:status` · `watchdog:status` · `schedule:inventory` · `autoloop:status` · `improvements:watchdog-status` · `dev:stall_waker_status` · `operator:trigger_state` · `plugins:runtime_status` | 216 |
| F | what is the pot / harness doing? | `pot:status` · `harness:status` · `curation:state-of-pot` · `autonomy:graduation_status` | 225 |
| G | local / UI / demo | `ui:get_state` · `operator:credentials_status` · `voice:status` · `dev:state_counter` | 15 |
| H | work-item hygiene | `work_items:redundancy_status` | 1 |

Cluster A is the clearest case: **six doors onto one question**, four of which read the
same gateway `/stats` oracle. Cluster C is the one already solved — all five registered
cells project `dev:pipeline_position`, which is what the answer looks like when it works.

Two entries in the table are traps rather than duplication, and are called out in their
verdicts so nobody "fixes" them:

- **`deploy:status` is not `deploy.3070.sha`.** The names rhyme; the questions do not.
  `deploy:status` reads a *harness's* deployment record and frame handle. The cell reads
  the *operator release* pipeline. Merging them on name similarity would be a real
  regression.
- **`schedule:inventory` is not a target — it is the precedent.** It is a catalog of
  every scheduled thing, and it is already the single anti-sprawl door for its own
  domain. This plan generalises what it did; it does not replace it.

## What has actually been retired so far

One entry, deliberately: **`dev:pipeline_position`**, taking `BASELINE` from 38 → 37.
It was the free one — it is *already* the resolver behind all five registered cells, so
declaring `@cell-lens git.pipelinePosition` cost one comment and moved it onto the
intended path. Its verdict survives in `VERDICTS` with an `adopted` note.

Retirement is staged on purpose. The gating deliverable of P-020 is the inventory and the
verdicts; the remaining adoptions are ordinary work, and each one now has a written target
and a mechanism that makes the shrink visible on every gate run:

```
✓ no UNDECLARED state-read tool — 39 state-read tool(s) in scope · 37 grandfathered …
  P-020 inventory: 38 tool(s) verdicted — 7 become a cell · 8 delegate to one · 23 stay
  bespoke; 1 adopted so far, 37 still grandfathered.
```

**To retire the next one:** register its cell(s) in
`packages/operator-core/lib/cell-registrations.ts`, add `// @cell-lens <cell.id>` inside
the tool's `defineTool({ … })` literal (the marker must be *inside* the literal — ownership
is attributed to the enclosing call), delete its `BASELINE` entry, and add an `adopted`
note to its verdict. The gate will tell you if you missed a step.

## The limitation this inventory has, stated rather than papered over

The inventory covers what the gate's signature selects, and that signature is **syntactic
over the tool name**. It misses state reads with unremarkable names — and the miss is
larger than the gate's own header suggests.

`fleet:assignments` is **the single most-called live-state read in the system — 5,883
calls across 5,851 distinct callers in 30 days**, roughly 9× `coord:presence`. It is not
in `BASELINE` and not flagged, because "assignments" is not in `STATE_NOUNS` — even though
it answers the canonical live-state question the coordination plane exists to answer.
Others missed the same way: `blender:success-metrics` (656), `facts:list` (584),
`coord:walls` (392), `locks:list` (245), `work_items:burn_down` (73), `pot:get` (50),
`coord:roster` (22), `coord:conditions` (16), `dev:pg_active_queries` (5).

Summed, the missed population is **7,926 calls against the whole baseline's 2,411** —
the reads the gate does not police are called more than 3× as often as the ones it does.

This does not make the gate wrong — its stated guarantee is narrow and precise ("the
state reads it *does* name cannot grow silently") and that guarantee holds. It bounds
what the guarantee is *worth*, and it bounds this inventory's completeness. Tracked as
**EI-18791777695307535**, with the recommendation that selection eventually invert from
naming to measured call volume, since that is the only variant that cannot be evaded by
choosing a different word.
